big_idea: Numbers help us answer 'how many', label things, measure stuff, and tell the time — they're everywhere in our classroom and our world.
learning_intention: We are learning that numbers are used for many different jobs, not just counting — they label things, measure things, and tell us when things happen.
student_learning_goal: I can find places where numbers are used in our classroom and tell why they matter.
success_criteria: I can find at least three different numbers around the classroom.
I can say what each number is for (counting, naming, measuring, or telling time).
I can name one job that numbers do in our every day.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart paper with four labelled columns: COUNTING — LABELS — MEASURE — TIME
One small clipboard per partner pair (~12 clipboards) with a printed 'Number Hunt' tracking sheet
Coco-the-Conductor-style classroom 'kitchen' apron for Mae and Theo (puppet/character introduction)
Optional: a wall clock, a wall calendar, a measuring tape — pre-positioned so children can find them

minds_on.hook: Today we welcome two new friends to our classroom: Mae and Theo, the Counting Crew chefs. They cook delicious snacks — but every recipe they make needs NUMBERS. They need YOUR help to find numbers all over the room.
minds_on.teacher_script: Bring children to the carpet. Hold up the Mae illustration in one hand and the Theo illustration in the other. 'Friends, meet Mae and Theo. They are the Counting Crew chefs in our classroom kitchen. They are baking cookies today, and they need a lot of numbers. How many cups of flour? How many cookies on the tray? How LONG to bake them? Without numbers, the cookies would not work.' Pause for a chuckle. Continue: 'But Mae and Theo just got here, and they don't know where the numbers in our classroom are. Look around — can you point to a number you can see right now?' Wait for hands. Take 3-4 quick answers, pointing or walking children to each spot. Listen for: clock, calendar, number line, page numbers in books, wall measuring chart, recycling-bin labels, ruler. As each is named, tape a sticky note on or near it that says NUMBER FOUND. The carpet should slowly fill with sticky-noted spots around the room. End by saying: 'Numbers are EVERYWHERE in our classroom — and every single one of them has a JOB. Today our job is to find as many numbers as we can, and figure out what each one is FOR.'
student_actions: Listen and watch as Mae and Theo are introduced.
Look around the room and raise hand when they spot a number.
Walk to the spot they pointed at when called on, and place the sticky note.
Notice how many sticky notes pile up by the end of Minds On.

steps.instruction: Whole group: introduce the Number Hunt clipboard. Show the tracking sheet with four boxes labelled COUNTING (cookies, fingers), LABELS (page numbers, recycling-bin numbers), MEASURE (rulers, weight scales, measuring tape), TIME (clock hands, calendar dates). Walk to one already-noticed number (e.g., the wall clock) and ask: 'What's this number for?' Take ideas, then sort it into TIME together. Repeat with one more (e.g., a page number in a picture book) — sort into LABELS.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Friends, your job is to be number detectives. Find a number, then ASK YOURSELF — is this for COUNTING, for LABELS, for MEASURING, or for TIME? Then draw or write where you found it in the right box.'

steps.instruction: Send partner pairs out with one clipboard between them. Pairs walk the classroom (and the hallway if safe) and find at least four different numbers, one for each box on their tracking sheet. They draw a quick sketch in the box (or write the spot if they can spell it).
steps.teacher_prompt: Walk pairs to their starting points around the room. Remind: 'You are looking for FOUR DIFFERENT JOBS — not just four counting examples. Look high up, look down low, look on the wall, look in your cubby.'

steps.instruction: Circulate and prompt with the diagnostic checklist. Watch for children who default to ALL counting examples (most common at K) — gently redirect them to look for time, labels, or measurement. Note which children spontaneously identify a non-counting use.
steps.teacher_prompt: Drop down to a pair's level. 'Show me what you have so far. Hmm — these are all counting things. Where in the room could you find a number that tells the TIME?' If they shrug, point at the clock, the calendar. 'And a measuring number?' Point at the height chart, the rain-stick markings, your ruler.

steps.instruction: Pairs return to the carpet with their clipboards. Anchor chart on the easel with the same four columns. Each pair shares ONE find — they tell where they found the number, and the class decides together which column it goes in. Teacher records on the chart with marker (write the spot, draw a tiny icon).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Pair-A, share your tricky one — the one you weren't sure about. Where did you find it, and what column should it go in?' Take pair contributions one at a time. If the class disagrees, GREAT — discuss WHY (e.g., the number on a school bus is BOTH a label AND a count of which bus number it is).

differentiation.for_emerging: Emerging children walk with a stronger partner; teacher hands them a 'starter card' showing one example per column to spark recognition. They contribute by pointing or naming, not necessarily writing.
differentiation.for_extending: Extending children find a FIFTH job a number can do that isn't on the chart (phone numbers, addresses, room numbers — these are typically labels but can prompt rich discussion). They start a fifth column on the back of the clipboard.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide picture-card prompts for each column header (clock-and-watch, page-number-and-book, ruler-and-tape, calendar-and-bus-number). Pre-teach 'count', 'label', 'measure', 'time' with hand gestures the child can echo while walking the room. Allow drawing instead of writing.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: The whole lesson IS the movement opportunity — pairs walk while hunting. For children who need additional regulation, they can carry a clipboard AND a small sandbag they place beside their spot when they find one.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Diagnostic-only at this stage. Note (a) which children spontaneously look beyond counting, (b) which children need redirection to non-counting examples, (c) which children can articulate the JOB a number does without prompting. These three signals predict where each child sits on the A6.1 progression entering Lesson 2.
formative_check.how_to_record: Class diagnostic checklist with rows for each child and three columns: 'identifies non-counting uses', 'articulates job', 'collaborates with partner on the hunt'. Tick as you observe.

discussion_prompts: Mae just asked us — could she bake cookies WITHOUT numbers? What would happen?
Theo wants to know — what was the most surprising number you found today? Where was it, and what was it for?
If our classroom did not have ANY numbers in it, what would be different? What would still work? What would break?
consolidation.exit_routine: On the way out the door, each child names ONE place in the room where they saw a number AND says one of the four jobs (counting, label, measure, time). Teacher tallies the four jobs to see if the class touched all of them or skewed to counting.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Anchor chart populated with class finds (collective evidence of which number-jobs the class recognised). Per-child diagnostic checklist with three indicators per child. Exit-routine tally showing distribution across the four jobs.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: A6.1 'explore what numbers are used for' is the BASELINE expectation for the unit. Children entering K vary widely — some can articulate that a clock-number means time; others see all numbers as counting. This lesson tests that baseline before Lessons 2-5 build on it.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When Every Find Is 'Counting' — redirecting toward labels, measurement, and time
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: The most common K trap on A6.1 is for the entire class to find only COUNTING examples — fingers, blocks, cookies, paper bears. The richer expectation is recognising that numbers ALSO label, measure, and tell time. Step 3 (circulate during the partner hunt) is where this redirect happens. The script below covers what to say and which physical objects to point at when a pair has filled all four boxes with counting examples.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Each pair has a Number Hunt clipboard with four boxes (COUNTING / LABELS / MEASURE / TIME). The teacher carries a diagnostic checklist clipboard and a pen. The classroom should have at least one VISIBLE example for each of the four jobs: a wall clock (TIME), a measuring tape or height chart (MEASURE), a recycling-bin number sticker or page numbers in a picture book (LABELS), and any quantity at all (COUNTING). If your room is sparse, pre-position one of each before Minds On.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script: Walk to a pair whose clipboard shows four counting examples (e.g., 'fingers — 5', 'cookies — 6', 'cubes — 10', 'bears — 4'). Crouch to their level. 'Wow, four numbers — great hunting. Tell me what each one is for.' Wait. They will probably say 'counting' for all four. Affirm: 'Yes, those are all counting numbers. Let us see if we can find a number that does a DIFFERENT job. Look up — can you see the clock?' Most children will. 'What numbers are on the clock?' They might say 1 through 12. 'And what is the clock telling us right now?' Wait for 'the time' or a guess. 'Yes — the clock uses numbers to tell us TIME. That is a different job from counting.' Have them draw the clock in the TIME box. Now point to a picture book on the table. Open it. 'See this little number in the corner of every page? That is a PAGE NUMBER. It tells us the page name — like a label. It is not counting how MANY pages we have read; it is NAMING which page we are on.' Have them draw a tiny page in the LABELS box. Move to MEASURE. Walk them to the height chart on the wall. 'Stand here. The numbers tell us how tall you are. That is MEASURING — they tell us SIZE, not just how many.' Have them draw the chart in the MEASURE box. Step back. 'Now your clipboard has all FOUR jobs. Tell me again — what jobs do numbers do?' Listen for the four words: count, label, measure, time. If they get all four, tick all three diagnostic columns on your checklist. If they hesitate on one, they are emerging on A6.1 — note that and circle back in Lessons 4 and 5.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Identifies four counting examples and says 'they are all for counting' — has not yet generalised that numbers do other jobs.
(Mid) After you walk them to the clock, they grasp TIME quickly but still need help finding LABELS or MEASURE.
(Strong) On their own, they articulate 'pages have names that are numbers — that is not counting'. Gets all four jobs unprompted.
(Stretched) Volunteers a fifth job — 'phone numbers are labels for people'. Recognises that one number can serve multiple jobs.
common_misconceptions: Every number is a counting number. (Child cannot yet separate quantity from label or measure or time. Most common K starting point.)
The clock numbers ARE counting (counting up to 12). (Child correctly notes 1-12 increases but does not grasp that the clock USES that sequence to tell TIME.)
Page numbers count how many pages you have read. (Child interprets the numeral as a quantity rather than a label or identifier.)
recovery_moves: Walk the child to a non-counting example physically. Do not describe it from the carpet — show them the clock face, the page corner, the height chart. Embodiment beats explanation at K.
Use the JOB framing every time. 'What JOB is this number doing?' Not 'how many is this?' — that question reverts the child to counting.

Anchor chart pairing. After redirecting one pair to the clock, take a photo with your phone of the clipboard with the new TIME entry. Add it to the anchor chart so the whole class sees the redirect succeed.

worksheet_brief.worksheet_title: Where Did You See a Number?
worksheet_brief.purpose: End-of-lesson consolidation. Children record one number-find per box on a four-quadrant page (COUNTING / LABELS / MEASURE / TIME). Captures the diagnostic-level evidence for A6.1 and creates a take-home conversation starter ('Show your family the four kinds of numbers you found today').

parts_outline.task: Draw or write where you saw a COUNTING number today.
Cut out the picture cards and sort them into the four columns: COUNTING, LABELS, MEASURE, TIME.
My favourite number today was _____ and it was for _____ .
